opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think that's a really important distinction, and it's one that sometimes gets blurred in discussions about whether neural networks "can" learn symbolic structure.

In a task like list reversal, or some of these other synthetic tasks people use, the structure is completely explicit in the data. Every training example is a perfectly clean instance of the rule. There's no noise, no ambiguity, and in a sense the task *is* the rule. So if a model fails to generalize there, say to longer lists or to symbols it hasn't seen in certain positions, that tells you something fairly direct about the model's inductive biases. And if it succeeds, that's encouraging, but it's a pretty narrow kind of success.

Natural language is a very different situation. The structure is there, and I'd argue it's pretty clearly hierarchical and in many ways symbolic, but it's never presented to the learner directly. You don't get sentences annotated with their syntactic trees. The structure is one of many things that could explain the input, and often the input is consistent with simpler, linear, surface-level generalizations. The classic example is subject-verb agreement or question formation in English. For a lot of the sentences a child, or a model, actually encounters, a rule like "agree with the closest noun" or "move the first auxiliary" works just fine. You only see the difference on the rarer, more complex sentences. So the question becomes: given data that's ambiguous between a structural generalization and a linear one, which does the learner pick? That's really a question about inductive bias under ambiguity, which is quite different from whether the model can represent the structure at all.

There's also the issue that in natural language, syntax is entangled with everything else: meaning, word frequency, plausibility, discourse. A model can get the right answer on an agreement test for the wrong reason, because some semantic or statistical cue happens to correlate with the right answer. So you have to be quite careful in designing evaluations to isolate the structural knowledge.

And then there's the scale. The synthetic tasks are small and you can control everything. With language, especially with modern language models, we're talking about enormous amounts of text, far more than any child gets. So even when a model does end up behaving as if it has learned hierarchical structure, you have to ask whether that's because it has a humanlike bias toward structure or simply because, with billions of words, it eventually saw enough of the disambiguating examples. That's part of why I've been interested in training models on more developmentally plausible amounts of data. It lets you ask whether the structure-sensitive behavior emerges from a learner with a reasonable amount of input, which is the question that matters if you care about human language acquisition.

So I'd say the synthetic tasks are useful as a controlled probe of what an architecture can do and what it's inclined to do, but they don't settle the question for language. The hard part in language is that the structure has to be inferred from messy, ambiguous, impoverished evidence, and that's exactly where you see differences between learners.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think of those as quite different problems, even though people sometimes lump them together under "does the model learn compositional structure."

With something like list reversal, the task is defined by a very clean, very small generalization. There's one rule, it applies uniformly, and crucially the training data is consistent with basically only that rule, if you've designed the experiment well. So the question you're asking is narrow: given a finite set of examples that are all compatible with "reverse the list," does the learner extract the rule itself, or does it extract some lookup-table-ish approximation that happens to agree with the rule within the range of lengths it's seen? That's what the length generalization experiments are probing. And the answer for standard architectures is often "it does something that looks right in distribution and falls apart when you go a bit longer." So those tasks are useful because they give you a very sharp diagnostic. You can't hide behind statistics there. Either you got the rule or you didn't.

Natural language is messier in a couple of ways that matter. First, the structure is there, but it's not the only thing in the data. A sentence has syntactic structure, but it also has a huge amount of lexical and collocational and world-knowledge regularity layered on top of it, and a lot of the time those lower-level cues are sufficient to get the right answer. So a model can get very far on agreement, on anaphora, on all kinds of things, using heuristics that are correlated with the structure without actually representing it. That's something we spent a lot of time on with subject-verb agreement. The model does well on average, and then you construct the cases where the heuristic and the structure come apart, and you see which one it was tracking.

Second, in language the "rule" isn't a single rule. It's a whole system of interacting generalizations, and the data underdetermines them in a way that's much closer to what the child faces. So the question isn't just "did it learn the rule," it's "which of many possible generalizations did it pick," and that's where inductive biases become the interesting variable. In the list reversal case the inductive bias question is mostly about whether the architecture can represent the rule at all in a way that extrapolates. In the language case the question is which of several representable hypotheses the learner prefers, given data that doesn't force the choice.

And then there's a third difference that I think gets underappreciated, which is that with natural language we actually have an independent theory of what the structure is. We have linguistics telling us what the generalizations look like, and we have human behavioral data showing what people actually do. So you can ask a much richer question: does the model's generalization match the human one? Not just "is it compositional," but "is it compositional in the specific way that human language is?" You can't really ask that about list reversal, because there's no human competence in list reversal that's independently interesting.

So I'd say the synthetic tasks are good for isolating a mechanism and getting a clear yes or no, and natural language is where you find out whether that mechanism, or whatever the model has instead, is actually the thing that explains human-like behavior. I don't think either one substitutes for the other. The mistake is treating success on one as evidence about the other.

astra-6.text:
I think the key difference is that in a task like list reversal, we know exactly what the underlying rule is. You get a sequence of symbols, and you need to output those same symbols in the opposite order. So we can ask a fairly precise question: did the model learn an operation that applies to arbitrary sequences, or did it learn something that only works for sequences similar to the ones it saw during training?

With natural language, identifying the structure is itself part of the problem. We don’t give the learner a set of clearly defined symbols and tell it what operation to perform. It has to discover useful categories and relationships from the input. And the input supports a lot of different generalizations, some of which might work very well on familiar sentences but fail in a new context.

So list reversal is useful as a controlled test of whether a model can learn a particular kind of systematic behavior. But learning that behavior doesn’t by itself tell us how the model would discover linguistic structure, or whether the structure it discovers is the same one people use. That requires a separate set of questions about what information is available in language and how learners generalize from it.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s an important difference in how clearly the task specifies the structure you’re trying to learn. With list reversal, you know exactly what the rule is: take a sequence of arbitrary elements and return them in the opposite order. You can then ask whether a model has learned that general operation or something that only works for the lengths and elements it saw during training.

With natural language, the structure isn’t handed to you in that way. You’re observing sentences, and there are many different kinds of regularities in those sentences—syntactic, semantic, statistical—that can help you make predictions. So even if a model performs well, it can be difficult to determine which regularity it’s using.

That’s why controlled tasks are useful: they let us isolate a particular capacity. But learning an explicitly defined operation and discovering useful abstractions from language are different problems. Success or failure on list reversal tells us something about a model, but we need an additional argument to connect that result to how it learns linguistic structure.
